classes.rule: A few verbs take an object and then the bare form of what the object does: let, make, have, help, see, watch, hear, feel. This is already the legend's makesdo list. The object is a nominal or an object pronoun, together with the place phrases and the "and"-joined nominals that hang on it. After such a verb and its object, the next word the text knows as a verb is the bare verb of a nonfinite clause whose subject is that object, tied to the governing clause. A bare "be" plus a participle there forms a passive nonfinite clause ("be turned"). That word is neither the head of the object's nominal nor a command of its own.

classes.name: A part of one sentence is tied to nothing (label before a dash, tag "would you", "missing: X", fronted or trailing phrase, clause after a dash)

classes.rule:
The words of one sentence (up to . ! ?) hang together. A clause or verbless group that no wire connects to the rest of its sentence, together with what hangs on it, is tied to the sentence's main clause by a relation without a marker. This is the judges' L6 test: tied to nothing inside its sentence.

Two exceptions:
- a group with no verb and no nominal holds only words said in passing (thanks, hey, next) and needs no tie;
- a clause whose own linking word the writer ties later is left alone.

classes.name: A comma alone, with no conjunction, coordinates an aside with a thing as if it were a second thing
examples: make a house, size 80 -> @k1 coordination conjunct=$n1 conjunct=$n2
a flower for me, 260 400 -> @k1 coordination conjunct=$n1 conjunct=$n3
My avatar, an old man, that is the figure I want. -> @k1 coordination conjunct=$n1 conjunct=$n2
hold off on the cat for now, hands off -> @k1 coordination conjunct=$n1 (the cat) conjunct=$n2 (hands)
classes.rule:
In English, a list of nominals joined by commas is closed by a conjunction before its last member (A, B and C). Where no conjunction closes the series, the nominal after a comma is not another member. It is an aside on what precedes it: an apposition, a property, a measure or a position. Tie it without a marker to the nominal before it, or to the clause when that nominal ends a relation. Lists of bare names keep their current treatment.

The same rule also removes the wrong comma-only coordinations in the 6 fronted if/while messages and in 2 "at y 90" messages: 21 comma-only coordinations in all, every one of them wrong.

classes.name: Count + plural unit + size word ("make tree 74 pixels wide")

Hey, make Tractor 2 62 pixels wide. -> @n1 nominal head="Tractor 2 62"

A word after such a measure that the text did not show as a thing (wide, tall, high) is a clause modifier, and the measure is a complement. About 1,400 dataset messages contain "N pixels wide".

classes.name: A verb in -s right after its subject read as the head of the subject's nominal
examples: ...on the side where the sun rises, and make it... -> @n5 nominal dependent="the" dependent="sun" head="rises"

classes.rule:
A clause needs a finite verb. Some stretches must be clauses: after a subordinator (where, until, because, while, when), after a colon, or at the start of a sentence. When such a stretch has no other verb, a word with the -s ending that closes a determiner-led nominal is its verb, and the nominal before it is its subject, even when the text does not know the stem as a verb (rises, owns, exits).

Also, a word in -s whose stem the text knows only as a verb (goes, wants) is the verb after the first nominal of a clause, including when the message starts with a lowercase word.

designs.approach:
Semi-supervised EM for the VSS station model. Each accepted circuit in the syntactic files is turned into a set of allowed stations per VSS token. The circuit key gives a role: verb, auxiliary, negation, clause modifier, discourse, nominal head, dependent before or after the head, marker of a relation to a nominal or to a clause, or conjunction. The role then maps to the legend stations that VSS's units turn into that role. The map is narrow, plus "wide" equivalences counted from data: in the cases where VSS's circuit equals the label, VSS's own path still puts 4.1% of heads at complement, 0.9% of verbs at auxiliary and 3.2% of clause modifiers at cue.

In the E-step of learnRoutes (src/routes.mjs), forward-backward runs inside these sets for labelled sentences, and their counts are weighted by λ. Unlabelled text keeps plain EM, so the result is a mixture of supervised and unsupervised counts. The same sets, applied at reading time, give an oracle: what VSS writes when its stations are forced to fit an accepted circuit. That oracle caps what any station-level lever can gain.

Code (scratch copy only, nothing in the repositories touched):
- /tmp/claude-1000/-home-salboaie-work-sopworlds/e235462f-8553-42ea-b357-85307b023a32/scratchpad/levers/prior/map.mjs: the circuit-to-station mapping.
- /tmp/claude-1000/-home-salboaie-work-sopworlds/e235462f-8553-42ea-b357-85307b023a32/scratchpad/levers/prior/vss/src/routes.mjs: the `supervised` option, a constrained and weighted E-step of about 30 lines.

designs.summary:
I built the lever end to end and measured it. It works, but the gain is small, because stations are not where most VSS errors come from.

**Mapping.** Accepted circuits map back to stations for 98 to 99.9% of word tokens. When VSS's stations are forced to the sets from a label, it reproduces that label in 98.7% of agreement labels (99.7% unforced), so the mapping is faithful.

**Ceiling.** On the benchmark, 538 messages are not accepted but have a known accepted circuit. For 54% of them, forcing VSS's stations to that circuit changes nothing: the stations already fit and the error is in units.mjs or links.mjs. Perfect stations would turn only 50 messages into accepted ones, which is +2.7 points (65.9% to 68.6%). A further 191 forced circuits are new and not yet judged; if about 30% of them passed, the ceiling would be about 71 to 72%.

**Trained models.** I trained scratch models with the prior. The benchmark's 1,745 labelled messages and a 3,731-message dev set were held out; 56,590 labelled messages were used. Measured only by known verdicts, they are flat or slightly lower (63.2 to 65.5% against 65.9% for the plain model retrained with the same code). They write 80 to 120 more circuits that no judge has seen.

**Estimate.** The best variant keeps the prior's station tables and the plain model's habits ("swap"). Counting circuits equal to an accepted one up to where a relation starts, and a 30% pass rate for new circuits, it gives about +1.4 points (range +0.6 to +1.9). It also comes closest to the accepted circuits: 3.84 differing lines on average against 3.97 for plain.

**Recommendation.** Do it only as a cheap add-on: about 6 to 9 hours, no word lists, and the reader stays the same. Confirm it with one judge packet of about 90 changed circuits first. The bigger levers are in units and links.

Suggested line for improvements-ideas.md: "VSS station prior from accepted circuits: +1.4 pt (estimate, 90 circuits to judge), ceiling of perfect stations +2.7 to 6 pt; 54% of VSS's failures already have the right stations, so units and links are the main target."
steps: 1. Port the mapping into strategies/vss as a training-time module, for example src/supervise.mjs. It holds the role-to-station sets plus the wide equivalences counted from data (head ~ complement, verb ~ auxiliary, clause modifier ~ cue). Add the `supervised` option to learnRoutes: constrained forward-backward over the allowed stations and a weight λ per labelled sentence. Add --supervise λ, --labels <syntactic dir> and --holdout <texts file> to train.mjs. The reader does not change.

2. Default training run: λ=1, all labels, narrow sets. Ship the supervised station tables (emission and shape, and optionally transitions) with the habits, prototypes, meanings and memory learned from the plain EM run. That is two EM passes, about 1.5 to 2.5 minutes more training. This 'swap' variant matched the fully retrained one (+1.4 points estimated each) with far fewer side effects: 11 accepted circuits change instead of 55, and there are no mass attachment flips.

3. Settle the uncertain part with one judge packet before adopting. Under 'swap', about 90 circuits change against plain (78 rejected to new, 11 accepted to new). Adopt only if the judged gain is positive. All other moves are known: 5 rejected become accepted, 2 accepted become equal-up-to-attachment.

4. Tackle the regression families seen, using only structure or the weights: command verbs lost at the start of a message ('focus on', 'Type "Draft"', 'write feeds'), verbs absorbed into names ('Rack meet', 'Bin match'), and participles made nominals ('colour-coded', 'coloured blue'). Tune λ, the mixture weight μ (50% tables gave +0.8 points estimated, with fewer changes), how wide each role's set is, and emission-only against full swap (emission-only +1.1, transitions-only +0.4 and almost risk-free). Rank variants on the held-out benchmark by the share of messages equal to an accepted circuit up to where a relation starts, by the mean distance to an accepted circuit, and by the dev labels.

5. Hold-out protocol. While the current benchmark is in use, hold its messages out of the supervision; 1,745 of the 1,831 now have labels, because the run rewrote them. When the benchmark is regenerated from the full data (owner's rule), measure with k-fold training (4 folds of about 2 minutes each), then train the final model on all labels.

6. Retrain after each judging round. The lever grows with judge-accepted labels on which VSS was wrong: today only 3,441 judge-accepted labels are usable outside the benchmark and dev set, and only 478 of them are circuits VSS did not write.

7. Put most of the effort elsewhere. In 54% of VSS's failures the stations already fit an accepted circuit, so the larger gains are in units.mjs and links.mjs: grouping nominals, choosing heads, finding the verb that opens a command.

designs.expectedGain:
About +1.4 points of accepted share on the random benchmark (central estimate), with a range of +0.6 to +1.9. The range depends on how a judge grades the roughly 90 circuits the prior changes (78 VSS rejections and 11 acceptances become new circuits).

Why it is small:
- With the current units and links, perfect stations add only +2.7 points with certainty, or about +3 to 6 points if new forced circuits pass at about 30%.
- In 54% of VSS's non-accepted messages the stations already fit an accepted circuit.
- The prior captures about half of that ceiling.
- Most fixes are one family: a quality word after a nominal becomes a clause modifier instead of the head of that nominal. That is the 'head <- complement' confusion, which accounts for most of the rejected-to-accepted moves. The regressions partly offset it.

Known verdicts alone show no gain (65.5% for swap against 65.9% for plain). The estimate rests on the not-yet-judged circuits.
designs.risks:
- **Self-training.** 91.7% of the labels (56,934 of 62,066) are circuits on which VSS and spaCy agreed, so they are VSS's own output. Most new information comes from the roughly 5,100 judge-accepted labels; only 478 of those outside the benchmark are circuits VSS did not write. The prior can entrench errors VSS shares with spaCy.
- **Contamination.** Each benchmark run rewrites the labels: 1,745 of the 1,831 benchmark messages now have one. Any supervised training must hold them out, or move to k-fold once the benchmark is regenerated from the full data.
- **Coupling with the later stages.** units.mjs, links.mjs, the doubts, the verb budget and the habits are tuned to how the EM model uses stations. Retraining everything with narrow sets flipped 40 accepted attachments and caused regressions. The 'swap' variant limits this, but command verbs at the start of a message and verbs absorbed into names still regress.
- **Uncertain measurement.** The gain depends on about 90 circuits no judge has seen. My 30% pass estimate is an informal reading of 38 examples.
- **Mapping blind spots.** Some accepted structures cannot be written with VSS units (a pronoun with "else"; a dependent after the head, as in 'outline gold'), so about 2% of tokens in the hard group get no supervision.
- **Low ceiling.** Even a perfect tagger adds only a few points; the work is better spent on units and links.
designs.effort:
About 6 to 9 hours in total:
- Port into strategies/vss (training module, the routes.mjs option, train.mjs flags, a hold-out file) and a small test: 2 to 3 h.
- Build one judge packet of about 90 changed circuits and read the verdicts: about 1 h plus judge time.
- Tune λ, μ, set width and emission-only against full swap: 2 to 3 h. Each run is about 2 minutes of training and 12 s of benchmark scoring, so 5 or 6 runs fit side by side; my 6 trainings ran in parallel in about 2.5 minutes.
- Regression families: 1 to 2 h.
- Each retraining after a judging round: about 5 minutes.
designs.fitsConstraints:
- **No word lists.** The lever adds none. The mapping names only schema keys (verb, auxiliary, head, dependent, marker and so on) and the stations of the legend. The wide equivalences are counted from data, not written by hand.
- **Training data.** Everything VSS gains about open-class words comes from training on accepted circuits, which the owner allows. No case from the dataset is hard-coded.
- **Portability.** The reader is unchanged at runtime. The model JSON keeps its format and size (3.2 to 3.4 MB) and still loads in a browser with no dependencies. Only training reads the syntactic CSV files and uses lib/syntax.mjs (validateSyntax, wordsOf).
- **Owner's other rules.** It follows "no JS patches" (a learned prior, no special cases) and "use all corpus lines" (the final model trains on all labels once the benchmark is regenerated; until then, measure with hold-out or k-fold).
- **This study.** Nothing under soplang-nlu or webmeet-dataset was edited, no git was used, and model/model.json was not overwritten. designs.approach: I replaced rules that use thresholds with small learned classifiers that sit on top of the existing rules. Each classifier gets the rule's own choice as one input, so it learns when to overrule the rule. Training data comes from the accepted circuits, aligned to VSS's units by word position. I tested two of the four named decisions offline, with the 1,831 benchmark messages held out: which earlier thing a listed thing joins (the coordination partner), and whether a word right after a thing names it or says how it is. The scorer is a JSON map of 125 to 262 weights and the score is a dot product, so VSS stays portable JavaScript with no dependencies. The main finding: the decisions get clearly better (errors down 30 to 40%), but the benchmark gain is small today (+0.1 to +0.3 points). There are two reasons. The labels mostly repeat VSS's own choices, so there is little to learn that VSS does not already do. And most rejected messages have two or more independent errors, so fixing one decision rarely makes the whole circuit acceptable. The plan therefore pairs the learned decisions with labels that correct VSS where it is wrong, and covers all the decision types together.
designs.summary:
Ranking the decisions by the rejections they cause, using 539 of VSS's 625 rejected benchmark circuits that have an accepted circuit to compare with (the first decision on which they differ):
- which word is the verb: 182, decided by the tagger and the "doubts" that make it read again
- a word right after a thing, taken as part of the nominal or as a clause modifier: 126
- coordination: 80
- nominal boundaries: 55
- clause form: 34
- head: 26
- where a relation with a marker starts: 14

Counting only messages with a single kind of error, the ceilings are: nominal grouping 112, coordination 80, verb 31, form 26.

Offline results, benchmark held out:
- Coordination partner, among benchmark cases where an accepted circuit lists the new thing with one of the earlier things: the current rule gets 283 of 307 right.
  - Trained on labels only: 285.
  - Trained on spaCy's circuits plus labels: 293, with 10 fixed and 0 broken.
- "Names it or says how": the rule gets 1,968 of 2,021 right. Trained on labels only: 1,988, with 24 fixed and 4 broken.
- Both plugged into a copy of VSS and run end to end (baseline 1,207 accepted):
  - safest setting (only overrule the rule when the classifier is confident): +4 accepted for certain, +1 probable, none lost (+0.3 points)
  - labels only: +2 (+0.1 points)

Why the gain is small: the labels VSS and spaCy agreed on make the same partner choice as VSS's rule in 5,249 of 5,251 cases (99.96%). So "training on labels" today mostly means training on VSS's own output. The plan has three phases:
1. Ship the two learned decisions behind a confidence threshold.
2. Get labels that correct VSS where it is wrong, by having judges grade the messages where VSS and spaCy disagree at these decision points. Then learn where a thing that is not listed should hang.
3. Bring the verb decision and the nominal boundaries into the same mechanism.

Rough expected gain: +0.3 points measured for phase 1, and about +1.5 to 3 points over several judged rounds for the full plan. The second figure is an estimate, not a measurement.
steps: 1. Add a decision recorder to VSS, in study mode with no change in behaviour (about 4–6 h). At each decision point it writes the candidates, their features and the rule's choice: partner() and the set-aside branch in fill(), attach(), the clause form, and the 'word after a thing' boundary. A hook lets a learned choice replace the rule's. This exists as a working copy in the study folder: vss/src/links.mjs, plus context.newPass so that only the final reading is recorded.

2. Extract training data by aligning VSS units to label wires (about 3 h; done in extract.mjs, gold.mjs and quality-extract.mjs). Tokens are mapped to words by character position (wordsOf). A VSS thing is matched to the label nominal that contains its head word. The answer for a partner decision is the earlier thing whose nominal is a conjunct of the same coordination; the other answers are 'none' (not listed), 'other' or 'unaligned'. This failed to align in only 2 of about 5,700 label cases. Use the labelled messages minus the benchmark, and weight judge-accepted circuits 10 to 20 times more than VSS–spaCy agreement circuits.

3. Make 'names it or says how' a learned doubt in the reader (about 6–8 h). It is a logistic classifier over the learned word habits (kindsOf counts for the word and the word before it, together(), saysHow, gradedForm, sForm, formOf), the -s and -ly endings, word shapes, the determiner, the nominal's role, whether the verb takes a quality, and the next word or punctuation, plus the rule's own choice. Where the classifier disagrees, the reader reads the sentence again with a doubt on that word: {is:'head'} or a new {is:'quality'}. Only overrule the rule when the score is above a margin of 2. Never apply it across punctuation. Add guards for words the legend lists, -ly words and fixed phrases such as 'side by side', which are the remaining breaks.

4. Make the coordination partner a learned choice (about 4–6 h). It is a softmax over the earlier things, with features: the rule's pick, alike(), meaning similarity, introduced alike (opener), nearest and distance, ends a phrase with a linking word, the role that holds it, already in a group, the linking word of its phrase (a preposition), determiner, name, number and plural agreement, comma-only joiner, and whether a later 'and' closes the series. It only chooses among the candidates; the rule's 'set aside' decision stays as it is.

5. Store the weights in model.json (about 16 KB) through train.mjs --out <scratch>, written in plain JavaScript with no dependencies (about 4 h). Measure with vss-registry.mjs on the benchmark and vss-accepted.mjs on 8,000 labels to catch regressions. In my in-sample check, 20 of 9,294 labels were lost and 1 gained; most losses were words like 'light' that can be a thing or a quality.

6. Get labels that correct VSS where it is wrong (about 3–4 h of design, plus judge time; the orchestrator launches the judges). spaCy circuits exist for 182k messages (eval-results/conversion/*/spacy-direct.jsonl). Pick the messages where VSS's decision disagrees with spaCy's: 2,627 disagreements on partner choice, 10,853 on whether to list at all, and about 7,200 on 'names it or says how'. Send a few hundred of them to the judge each round. The accepted circuits become labels, which the owner allows as training data, and the models are retrained. The owner decides whether spaCy's circuits, or spaCy and DistilBERT agreeing, may also be used directly as training data without a judge.

7. Add a second learned decision for a thing that is not listed: where it hangs (about 8–10 h). The options are a complement of the clause, a tie from the nearest thing, or a tie from the clause. Then turn on the 'none' option for the partner. The measured decisions improved from 297 to 332 of 368, but end to end 19 to 27 accepted circuits became unjudged, because VSS's way of writing a set-aside thing (a tie from the clause) does not match what accepted circuits do.

8. Bring the remaining decisions into the same mechanism (about 12–16 h). The verb decision is the largest family (182 rejections as the first error). Next come the nominal boundary (a word that begins another thing: 63 errors among those decisions on the benchmark), then clause form (34) and where a relation starts (14).

9. After every judged run, retrain from the corrected labels and re-measure on a freshly drawn benchmark (about 1 h per round). The rule's choice is an input to every model, so models must also be retrained whenever someone changes a rule. This applies now: the other agent's list-after-place-phrase rule targets the same partner errors.

designs.expectedGain:
Measured: about +0.3 points on the benchmark for phase 1 (+4 to +6 accepted messages for certain, with none lost at the confidence margin), or +0.1 to +0.2 points if training may use only labels. The decisions themselves improve much more: partner errors fall from 24 to 14 and 'names it or says how' errors from 53 to 33.

The benchmark moves little for three reasons:
- The errors fixed sit mostly in long scene descriptions that have other errors too: 290 of 539 rejected messages have two or more kinds of error.
- Reading the sentence again can change other words as a side effect.
- The labels contain almost no cases where VSS was wrong.

Estimate for the full plan, not measured: if every decision type is covered and corrected labels arrive through judging, and each type's errors fall by about 30 to 40% (as measured here), then a share of the 285 messages with a single kind of error (nominal grouping 112, coordination 80, verb 31, form 26, other 36) would become acceptable. Allowing for the low conversion seen here, that is about +1.5 to 3 points (roughly 30 to 55 messages) over several judged rounds. The upper end requires the verb decision to be learned as well.
designs.risks:
- Training only on labels largely reproduces the rules, because the labels came mostly from VSS agreeing with spaCy (measured at 99.96%). Without labels that correct VSS where it is wrong, the gain stays near zero.
- spaCy's circuits follow spaCy's conventions. A model with the 'none' option trained on them got worse when judged only against accepted circuits that are not spaCy's (203 → 193 of 219). Use spaCy's circuits only for the partner choice, or only after a judge confirms them, and only if the owner agrees.
- Reading the sentence again can change neighbouring words: 3 accepted circuits were lost with no margin, 0 with the margin of 2. Margins and guards are needed.
- Fixing one decision rarely makes a whole circuit acceptable. The gain only appears when several decision types are learned together.
- The other agent is changing VSS right now (rules for lists after place phrases, two participles in a row, and more). These target the same partner errors, so the learned partner's gain may shrink and the models must be retrained after their change.
- The evaluation is uncertain: 132 to 175 changed circuits have no verdict yet. My 'probable' estimate is a heuristic, and a judge should grade the changed circuits before anything ships.
- Near-identical template messages appear in both training and benchmark (for example 'make X N pixels wide'), so the measured gain may overstate how well this generalises. The owner accepts this for now.
- Features that name individual open-class words would memorise dataset cases. Keep the features free of such words.

designs.approach: The lever: let spaCy and DistilBERT (the "teachers") tell VSS how each word is used, as evidence that VSS reads again with, not as a reranker. A small per-word table (hashed logistic weights, plain JS) learns from teacher circuits on the corpus which of five classes each word belongs to: verb, nominal word, modifier, marker, other. Where the table is sure (p>0.9) and VSS's reading disagrees, the word is kept off the stations that class rules out, and VSS reads the message again with its own doubt loop, linker and writer. In Node only, an optional second mode applies when teacher circuits are passed in at run time: VSS returns the one of its own alternative readings that equals a teacher circuit. I measured a whole-circuit reranker and do not recommend building it now: VSS's own alternatives rarely contain an accepted circuit.
designs.summary:
Choosing among VSS's own readings is capped at about +5 points. Its 6 to 14 alternatives per message hold a known-accepted circuit in only 70.5% to 71.6% of messages, against 66.4% for its first reading. A portable reranker trained with a spaCy teacher gave no net gain. Even when the stations, attachment hosts and coordination partners were forced to match an accepted circuit, only 88 of 539 rejections were known to be fixed; 331 more changed to circuits no judge has read.

The lever that does reach VSS's errors is teacher evidence about how each word is used. A word table distilled from spaCy circuits halves VSS's noun-or-verb errors per word (99.46% against 98.79% agreement with accepted circuits). Used as evidence it changes 350 of VSS's 625 rejected circuits but only 57 of its 1,206 accepted ones. Known gain: +1.1 points (67.0%). Estimated gain: +3 to +6 points, depending on how many of the 325 changed circuits no judge has read would pass. In Node, with teachers present, VSS reaches 70.3% on known verdicts alone.

The dataset's accepted circuits alone teach nothing here: they were selected where VSS already agreed, and VSS's first reading equals the label in 98.8% of 25,200 labelled messages. So the teacher circuits must first become accepted labels, settled where spaCy and DistilBERT agree and audited by a judge. That needs the owner's consent.

Everything is in /tmp/claude-1000/-home-salboaie-work-sopworlds/e235462f-8553-42ea-b357-85307b023a32/scratchpad/levers/model-evidence/. It holds the scripts, a patched VSS copy in vss/ (snapshot of 17:04 with its own model; reader.mjs and links.mjs have the study hooks), the results, and judge packets in to-judge/. Nothing in the repositories was changed.
steps: 1. Settle the training data the owner's way (data step, about 2 h plus GPU and CPU time). Run DistilBERT (GPU, about 15 min) and the spaCy strategy over the unlabelled messages. spaCy-direct circuits already exist for 182k messages under eval-results/conversion/*/spacy-direct.jsonl, but the benchmark's spaCy is the former spacy-beam. Settle the circuits where the two agree as labels in syntactic/, with an audit share read by a judge (round.mjs settle --families 2). On the benchmark that agreement was accepted 539 of 542 times. It covers about 11% of the messages that had no label (135 of 1,238), roughly 13k corpus messages, all of them messages where VSS differs. Without this step the table has nothing to learn from: trained on labels alone it reaches 98.70% per word against VSS's 98.79%.

2. Add an evidence input to VSS (about 1 h). analyse(text, {evidence}) takes, per word, a distribution over verb / nominal word / modifier / marker / other. Where the most probable class has p>0.9, differs from VSS's reading and is not 'other', the word is kept off the stations that class rules out, and the normal doubt loop runs. The prototype is 5 lines in reader.mjs (extra.bans) plus the class-to-station map in model-evidence/distil-roles.mjs.

3. Train the distilled word table (about 2-3 h). Use a five-class hashed logistic model over function-word and structure features: the word, endings, capitals, the words around it, punctuation before and after, position. Train on the accepted circuits of syntactic/, now including the settled teacher-agreement circuits, and leave the 1,831 benchmark messages out. Store it quantised (2^18 buckets x 5 classes as int8 is about 1.3 MB) beside model.json; train.mjs writes it with --out. In the prototype, training took 54 s in plain JS on 4.86M word updates.

4. Have a judge read the circuits nobody has graded yet before trusting the gain: model-evidence/to-judge/packet-distil-roles.jsonl (325 circuits) and packet-distil-verb.jsonl (247), with the keys in key-*.jsonl. The rate at which these pass decides whether the lever is worth +2 or +6 points. Then tune the 0.9 threshold to trade the 35 accepted circuits that changed against the rejected ones that changed.

5. Optional Node mode (about 1 h). Promote the prototype k-best block in reader.mjs (attachment flips, each uncertain word banned and re-read with the doubt loop, the k-best station paths). When teacher circuits are passed in, return the alternative equal to one of them, up to the start of marked relations (relaxedCore). It is off by default and never runs in the browser.

6. Extend the evidence to cut decisions (about 3-5 h). Add two more distilled tags per word: 'starts a new nominal / continues the one before' and 'starts a clause'. units.mjs would consult them at its cut points. Wrong nominal grouping is the second most common first difference between VSS's rejected circuits and accepted ones (122 of 539, after the verb at 188).

7. Leave for later: tables for the attachment host and the coordination partner (the hooks exist in my links.mjs copy). Even perfect choices there fix only 18 and 19 of 539 rejections on their own, 26 together. Also leave the whole-circuit reranker: its ceiling is +4.8 to +5.2 points with today's alternatives, and the trained version gave no net gain.
8. Re-run the 1% benchmark and report L8+L9+L10 for VSS with evidence and without it, in browser mode (table only) and in Node mode (teachers present).

designs.expectedGain:
Browser VSS (table only): +1.1 points on known verdicts (65.9% to 67.0%). The estimate with unread circuits is +3 to +6 points, about 69-72%. If about 20% of the 290 changed rejected circuits pass, and the 35 changed accepted circuits pass at the same rate, the share is about 70.6%. The gain comes from the targeting: when the table disagrees with VSS it is usually VSS that is wrong (86% of the changes fall on rejected circuits). Re-reading also leaves VSS's linker to fix what follows from the corrected word.

Node with teachers at run time: +4.4 points on known verdicts (70.3%), about +5-6 with the re-read as fallback.

It stays well below spaCy (82.5%). Most of VSS's remaining errors sit in cutting and linking: even perfect stations, hosts and partners fix only 88 known plus an unknown share of 331. Step 6 (distilled cut tags) is the next increment. Some of the gain may overlap with rules the other agent is adding now: participles, a comma between two numbers, place-phrase lists.

- Size: the prototype is 20 MB in float32; it must be hashed smaller and quantised for the browser.
- Measured on a 17:04 snapshot of VSS; the other agent's edits will shift the base.
- The whole-circuit reranker looks unpromising; that finding could change if link-level alternatives are added later.

rules.rule: Inside one sentence (up to . ! ?), two parts kept apart only by a comma, dash or semicolon, each either a clause with its verb or a fragment holding a nominal, with no conjunction and no linking word: write a coordination with no conjunction (the lever P form, which judges accepted from spaCy in labels). After that, any group still tied to nothing gets a relation without a marker from the first finite clause of the main group (the P2 pass). Three exemptions: a group with no verb and no nominal (discourse only); a fronted subordinate clause, which hangs on the part after it (R10); a participle that tieLoose already ties.

rules.name: R2 Causative verb + object + bare verb is a nonfinite clause (merged: drawing makesdo 14 + diagram CAUSATIVE 5 + LETS 3)
rules.rule: After a verb of the legend's makesdo list (let, make, have, help, see, watch, hear, feel) and its object, the next word the text knows as a verb is the bare verb of a nonfinite clause tied to the governing clause. The object is a nominal or object pronoun with its place phrases and its 'and'-coordination. The subject of the new clause is the whole object: the coordination, or the start of the 'of' chain. Adverbs and 'not' between 'let's' and the verb are skipped. A bare 'be' plus a participle makes a passive. P1's guards stay: determiner-led object, no 'of' after the word, no quality after a takesQuality verb, not a listed, graded or quality word. A participle after need/want/like plus an object is the same clause shape. The rule names only common verbs.

rules.name: R3 A noun that describes the next noun continues the nominal (merged: diagram COMPOUND 20 + docal lever N 5)
rules.rule: After the noun of a nominal, or after a capitalised name with no determiner, a word the text knows as a thing continues the nominal, and the last noun is the head. 'Knows as a thing' comes from learning: kindsOf/nominal(), not saysHow, not listed, not a verb form. It continues in two cases: another such word follows, or it is the last word before a linking word or a break and no takesQuality verb is waiting for it. It stops after a plural noun, at listed words and at words learned as describing.

Checked: COMPOUND changes 2 of 2,000 and 4 of 8,000 accepted circuits (1 worse: 'brick red'); N changes 0 of 10,685 labelled messages with the pattern. N's one raw regression ('Home whichever way') goes away once 'whichever' is in the legend.

rules.name: R4 A describing word after a nominal is neither its head nor a verb (merged: drawing 'quality after object or be' 9 + diagram TRAIL_QUALITY 12 + drawing 'with + nominal + describing word' 8)
rules.rule: A word the text shows as describing at least as often as naming, right after the noun of a nominal, is not the head. After a subject or complement it is a modifier of the clause; at the end of a relation with a marker it is a dependent (Rule 5.2, 'with outline gold'). Right after a form of 'be', a bare form makes no verb group. After 'with' and a nominal, a describing word with no object after it is said of that nominal. Nothing inside a 'with' phrase is a finite clause.

rules.name: R5 The opening word of a sentence part: command verb or heading (merged: diagram CMD_VERB 13 + docal lever Q 3)
rules.rule: A part starts at the message start, after a break, after 'so'/'then' that follows a break, or after an opener. Its first word is the command verb when a determiner or an object pronoun follows it directly and the text has seen the word as a verb. This never applies to an -s form or a plural, or when a finite verb follows before the next break. The reverse case: one or two opening words closed by a comma or dash, followed by a clause with a known verb, never seen as a verb, and with no object after them, form a fragment (a heading, a name or a word said to the listener).

rules.name: R6 The finite verb by subject-verb agreement (merged: drawing '-s verb after its subject' 7 + SUB_VERB 9 + DECL_START 4 + 'subject with a place phrase' 3 + AND_SUBJECT 3 + docal lever S 3 + AS_OPENER 3)
rules.rule: Some stretches must hold a clause: after a subordinator, after a colon, or after a question word inside a message. In such a stretch with no other verb, an -s form that closes a nominal whose noun is singular is its verb, and the nominal with its place phrases or coordination is the subject. A bare present form does not follow a singular subject. Whether a noun is singular or plural must be a habit learned from raw text (is/are, was/were and -s verbs after the noun), not a hand rule.

rules.name: R7 A numeral or 'one/ones' with no noun after it is the head (merged: drawing 'one' 4 + diagram ONE_HEAD 9)
rules.rule: 'one'/'ones', or a spelled numeral, with no noun after it and standing after a determiner, a selector or a quality, heads the nominal; the words before it are dependents. A determiner-word (that, this, which, each) right before a noun or 'one' is its determiner, unless that noun is followed by its own verb. A number right after a noun ('block 2') is unaffected.

rules.name: R8 'else' after an indefinite pronoun or a question word belongs to it
rules.rule: 'else' right after an indefinite pronoun (everything, anything, nothing, something, everyone, anyone, someone, nobody, somebody, anybody, everybody) or a question word (what, who, where) is a dependent of that nominal.

rules.name: R9 Where a number goes (merged: drawing 'number after a noun' 5 + diagram ATTR_VALUE 4 + drawing 'count + plural unit' 7)
rules.rule: A number right after a noun, a single letter or a property word belongs to it (Rule 5.5). After a noun and its number, a bare noun opens the next pair. A cardinal right before a plural noun counts that noun and begins a new nominal, which the plural closes; this is tested by the -s ending, not by the station. After a naming verb, the noun and its number together are the name.

rules.name: R10 A fronted subordinate clause hangs on the part after its comma (merged: drawing fronted if/while 6 + diagram SUB_ATTACH 5)
rules.rule: A clause opened by a subordinator at the start of the message or after a dash, semicolon or colon ends at its comma. It hangs on the part that follows (a clause or a fragment), with its subordinator as the marker. It is never a conjunct, it never hangs on the clause before it, and no coordination reaches across its comma. It is not cut when a list closed by 'and' follows before the next verb.

rules.name: R12 Participles: after a comma, after a nominal that is already held, after 'be' (merged: diagram PART_COMMA 12 + PART_NOUN 7 + BE_PART 5)

A form of 'be' followed, after a complete subject, by an -ing form or a past form of a known verb is the auxiliary.

rules.name: R14 A coordination joins alike, adjacent conjuncts (merged: drawing 'and' inside a place phrase 6 + diagram COORD_LIKE 4)

designs.approach: Design 1: a semi-supervised EM station prior from accepted circuits (the 'swap' variant: supervised station tables, plain habits). Scales: higher gain = more gain, higher risk = more risk, higher effort = more work, higher fit = better fit.
designs.evidenceHolds: Only in part. These parts hold: the mapping is faithful (98.7% of forced readings reproduce the label), and the oracle ceiling is right (+2.7 pt strict; in 54% of failures the stations already fit). The +1.4 pt claim does not rest on known verdicts: accepted circuits fall from 1,207 to 1,200 (-0.4 pt), so the whole gain comes from an assumed pass rate for 197 unread circuits. The author's own reading supports about 32% for rejected-to-new (12 of 38), but only 5 of 13 (about 38%) for accepted-to-new, against the 50% the estimate assumes. 91.7% of the supervision is VSS's own output, so there is little new signal. Only the transitions-only variant (+0.4 pt, 124 new circuits) is close to risk-free.
designs.verdict: Defer. Judging the existing packet of about 90 swap circuits costs no code, so do it in parallel now. Adopt transitions-only or swap only if the judged net is positive, and only after the judged loop has added labels where VSS was wrong (478 today). Build at most one of designs 1 and 3, since both act on stations.

designs.approach: Design 2: learned per-decision classifiers on top of the rules. Each takes the rule's choice as an input, uses features from structure and learned habits only, and is stored as about 16 KB of dot-product weights in model.json. Coordination partner and 'names it or says how' were tested; a decision recorder and judge packets on VSS-spaCy disagreements are the plan.
designs.evidenceHolds: The decision-level gains hold, with the benchmark held out: partner 283 to 293 of 307, and 'names it or says how' errors 53 to 33 of 2,021. The phase-1 +0.3 pt (+4 to +6 messages) needs spaCy circuits as partner training data, which are not accepted circuits. Labels alone give +2 messages (+0.1 pt). The in-sample check lost 20 and gained 1 of 9,294 labels. The +1.5 to 3 pt for the full plan is an unmeasured extrapolation; it depends on judged disagreement packets producing labels where VSS was wrong. The diagnosis is solid: the first differing decision is verb 182, word after a nominal 126, coordination 80, nominal boundary 55.
designs.verdict: Adopt in part, in step 3. The recorder and extraction become the measuring tool for every rule. Ship the 'names it or says how' classifier (labels only, margin 2) as the learned form of R4, after R3 lands, and retrain it after every rule change. The judged disagreement packets (phase 2) are the best source of new labels for every learned lever, and that loop is the owner's stated strategy. Learn the verb decision (phase 3) only after R6's agreement habit exists.

designs.approach: Design 3: teacher evidence. A hashed per-word table with five classes, distilled from spaCy/DistilBERT circuits, bans stations where it is confident (p > 0.9), and VSS reads the message again with its own doubt loop. There is an optional Node mode with teachers at run time.
designs.evidenceHolds: The known +1.1 pt holds only for a table trained on spaCy circuits from 181k messages. Under the owner's rule (accepted circuits only), the labels-only table gives 66.1% (+0.2); labels plus 13k spaCy circuits give +0.8. The +3 to 6 pt estimate rests on a 20% pass rate the author read on 34 circuits, applied to 290 unread circuits. The upper end needs about 40%, and nothing supports that. The 70.3% Node figure needs teachers at run time. Targeting is genuinely good: 86% of the changes fall on rejected circuits. The oracle agrees with design 1: perfect stations, hosts and partners fix only 88 known messages.
designs.verdict: Conditional. Send the existing packets (325 + 247 circuits) to the judge now, in parallel; this needs no code. Build the browser table (2^18 x 5 int8, about 1.3 MB) only if at least 25% pass and the owner allows spaCy-and-DistilBERT agreement to be settled as labels with a judge audit. Drop Node mode and the reranker. If both conditions hold, prefer this design over design 1.

plan: Step 0, now, alongside the other agent. (a) Judging that needs no VSS code: the orchestrator sends design 3's packets (levers/model-evidence/to-judge, 325 + 247 circuits) and design 1's swap packet (about 90 circuits) to the judge. The verdicts decide step 4 and add judged circuits to the registry. (b) When the other agent's batch lands, take one stable copy and rebaseline: vss-registry.mjs on 2026-11-27-syntax-benchmark-random, and vss-accepted.mjs at --size 2000 and 8000. Write the remaining count per class into the journal. Every prototype above was built on an older snapshot, so all line numbers move.

Step 1, first code group: the measured, low-damage prototypes, one commit per rule. R1 (lever P coordination, then the P2 fallback, with the R10 exemption stubbed until R10 lands), R2 (P1 plus the coordination subject and the let's adverb skip), R3 (COMPOUND + N) together with R13 (legend words, retrained to a scratch model and then adopted), R5 (CMD + Q), and R12's PART_COMMA. Port them in parallel in separate copies (their sites differ: linkSentence and tieLoose; links 228; units 268+ and readEntity; reader openers; units command rules), then merge in ranking order. Why first: all are prototyped, each changes 0 to 6 of 8,000 accepted circuits, and together they target about 74 judged faults. Measure: registry fixed/broken per class with each lever toggled off and on; vss-accepted at 2,000 and 8,000, reading every changed circuit (expect about 25, most of them added ties); then one judge packet of every changed unjudged circuit, including the roughly 31 L8 circuits that gain a tie (the L4 check). Expected: +1.5 to 2.5 pt, because about half of the repaired faults sit in messages with no other fault.

Step 2: the untried structural rules, after the other agent's list, participle and comma-number rules land, since they share the seriesU and participle code. Order: R10 (it must run before R1's coordination), R7, R8, R9, R11 (a revision of the existing likeness rule; check the 56 labels that hold a comma-only coordination), the rest of R12, R16, R14, R15, R17. Prototype each in its own copy in parallel and merge in ranking order. Measure as in step 1. Stop a rule that changes more than 0.5% of the 8,000 accepted circuits, or that breaks more than it fixes on the registry. Expected: +1 to 2 pt.

Step 3: learned decisions where thresholds fail. Port design 2's recorder and alignment. Train the 'names it or says how' classifier (labels only, margin 2) as the learned R4. Learn a singular/plural habit from raw text in habits.mjs (is/are, was/were, -s verbs after the noun) and build R6 on it instead of lever S. In parallel, the orchestrator sends judge packets of VSS-spaCy disagreements at these decision points, a few hundred per round, and the accepted circuits are added as labels; retrain after each round. Measure: decision accuracy on the held-out benchmark (the 2,021 'names it or says how' cases and the 307 partner cases), end to end through the registry plus a judge packet, and the 8,000 accepted circuits. Expected: +1 to 2 pt, rising as judged labels accumulate.

Step 4, only if step 0's verdicts justify it: station-level learning. If design 3's packets pass at 25% or more and the owner allows settling spaCy-and-DistilBERT agreement as labels with a judge audit, build the browser word table. Otherwise try design 1 transitions-only on the larger set of judged labels. Not both. Measure on a benchmark freshly drawn from the full data (owner's rule) with k-fold training, and report L8+L9+L10 with and without the lever. After every step, record the plan, the measured result and the open items in the journal and in improvements-ideas.md, and commit.
